headline: xAI data centers powered by 8 converted jet engines face pollution concerns
summary: Elon Musk's xAI is using repurposed jet engines to power a Mississippi data center, but environmentalists are raising alarms over increased pollutant emissions.
details: Elon Musk's xAI is reportedly powering a Mississippi data center with eight converted jet engine turbines. While the generators have state permits, environmental groups are concerned about increased emissions of volatile organic compounds and carbon monoxide.

The Southern Environmental Law Center has challenged Mississippi's approval, arguing that xAI has not guaranteed emissions standards are met and has potentially "undercounted" projected pollution. This follows a previous lawsuit over gas generators used without proper permits.

The turbines are converted by ProEnergy, which repurposes unused General Electric engines typically found on Boeing aircraft. This solution emerged as data center energy demand outpaces traditional utility capabilities.

Each turbine can produce up to 50 megawatts of electricity, enough to power approximately 15,000 homes. This addresses the critical need for power, as data centers are projected to consume 20% of U.S. electricity by 2035, with many buildouts delayed or canceled due to power shortages.

xAI, in particular, faces pressure to expand its data center capacity significantly, with Elon Musk aiming for a sevenfold increase by the end of 2027. Delays in power provision could jeopardize these ambitious plans.

The use of jet engines, while potentially addressing power supply issues, is unlikely to ease local concerns about pollution. Public sentiment towards data centers has already soured due to power and water usage issues.

headline_marked: NASA's [[Swift Observatory]] set for fiery re-entry into Earth's atmosphere
headline: NASA's Swift Observatory set for fiery re-entry into Earth's atmosphere
summary: After 22 years in orbit, the 3,200-pound space telescope is expected to burn up on Wednesday, with a low risk of any components reaching the ground.
details: NASA's Swift Observatory, launched almost 22 years ago, is scheduled to re-enter Earth's atmosphere on Wednesday. Attempts to boost its orbit failed, leading to its controlled descent.
The observatory is expected to re-enter around 3:30 AM ET, with a potential deviation of up to 11 hours. NASA anticipates that most of the spacecraft will disintegrate due to atmospheric friction.
Weighing approximately 3,200 pounds, the Swift Observatory measures 5.6 meters (18.4 feet) in height and 5.4 meters (17.7 feet) in width, including its solar arrays.

While most of the telescope is expected to burn up, some components may survive re-entry. NASA estimates the risk of harm to anyone on Earth is unlikely, with a probability of approximately 1 in 2,100.

The observatory's operational life far exceeded its initial two-year mission to study gamma-ray bursts. It later served as a general-purpose multi-wavelength observatory until solar storms affected its orbit.

NASA and the Space Force will continue to monitor the re-entry and provide updated predictions on potential impact locations, which are limited to between 20.6 degrees south and 20.6 degrees north latitude.
